    "/food/everyday/": "Start with a small bowl. Follow a fruit, a handful of badi, a leaf-wrapped parcel—and the people who make them memorable.",

descriptions./: Explore Odisha’s people, places, culture and opportunities. Find the knowledge to plan your visit or investment.
descriptions./404.html: Find your way back to Project Odisha’s stories, coastal guides and saved journey ideas.
descriptions./explore/: Find places, coastal food and stay-area guides in the first Project Odisha collection. Search by name, topic or place connection.
descriptions./journey/: Collect Odisha places and meals, arrange your days, add personal notes and download an offline tour book. Your plans stay in your browser.
descriptions./journey-starters/: Choose a city, coast or Chilika starting collection. Save ideas into a separate journey, arrange your own days and carry an offline tour book.
descriptions./about/: Why Project Odisha is building a shared encyclopedia of Odisha’s places, people and living heritage, one carefully told story at a time.
descriptions./founder/: Meet Ahimanikya Satapathy, Founder & Editor-in-Chief of Project Odisha, and the personal purpose behind this growing collection.
descriptions./contribute/: Help improve Project Odisha with a correction, a source or firsthand knowledge. Prepare a draft locally and choose whether to share it publicly.

descriptions./destinations/bhubaneswar/: Begin in Bhubaneswar: follow stories in stone, choose a few places to linger and connect the city with Dhauli and the Odisha coast.
descriptions./visit/places/dhauli/: Look closely at Dhauli’s layered landscape of remembrance and belief. Plan a thoughtful visit and continue towards Konark.
descriptions./knowledge/konark/: Explore Konark through its Sun Temple, carved details, coastal connections and food. Gather ideas for your own Odisha journey.
descriptions./destinations/puri/: Discover Puri through the shore, its living sacred traditions and food. Leave space for local rhythms and a visit to Raghurajpur.
descriptions./visit/places/raghurajpur/: Meet Raghurajpur through its craft tradition and village setting. Approach a visit with curiosity, respect and time to look closely.
descriptions./food/puri-coast/: A coastal table: explore Mahaprasad, fish, prawns and chhena poda with context and questions to ask before choosing your meal.
descriptions./visit/stays/puri-coast/: Compare Puri and Konark as bases for a coastal visit. Consider the setting, transport and facilities, then check a property directly.

descriptions./food/poda-pitha/: Discover Poda pitha through Raja, named preparations and the people behind them. Save a food story and questions for your Odisha journey.

descriptions./food/everyday/: Start with a small bowl. Follow a fruit, a handful of badi, a leaf-wrapped parcel—and the people who make them memorable.
descriptions./food/ou-khatta/: A little sweet, a little sour. The bowl at the edge of the meal has a story of its own.
descriptions./food/badi-chura/: A handful of crumbs, a generous amount of character. Meet the little accompaniment that deserves a closer look.
descriptions./food/tala-pitha/: A golden slice and a browned edge. Follow ripe palm fruit into one of Odisha’s seasonal food stories.
descriptions./food/fire-cooking/: A blistered vegetable, an opened leaf parcel, a browned edge. Follow the heat into three food stories—and leave room for the cook’s own version.
descriptions./food/baigana-poda/: A blistered skin gives way to a soft centre. Follow roasted eggplant from the flame to a small bowl beside the meal.
descriptions./food/tomato-poda/: A tomato meets the heat; a meal gains another small bowl. Discover the roasted accompaniment through one cook’s account.
descriptions./food/patrapoda/: Open a leaf parcel and the story changes with what is inside. Meet mushroom, fish and prawn preparations without treating them as one dish.
descriptions./crafts/: A cut piece of cloth. A brush held close. A silver thread bent into a pattern. Follow three crafts into the decisions—and the people—behind them.
descriptions./crafts/pipili-applique/: Colour catches your eye. A seam holds it there. Look closely at the cut cloth, the stitched edge and the person who brings the pattern together.
descriptions./crafts/pattachitra/: Before you try to understand the whole painting, follow one line. A border, a gesture, a tiny face can open a much larger story.
descriptions./textiles/: A pattern planned in yarn. A poem woven into silk. A colour drawn from roots. Follow Odisha’s textile stories into the materials, places and people behind the cloth.
descriptions./textiles/sambalpuri-bandha/: A peacock opens its tail across the cloth. Follow the pattern backwards, and you arrive at a bundle of yarn—and the decisions made before weaving began.
descriptions./textiles/khandua/: A page can be made of thread. In this Khandua, lettering moves across red cloth—an invitation to meet poetry, devotion and the people who weave them together.
descriptions./knowledge/kotpad/: Before a colour reaches the loom, there is another story to tell. In Kotpad, following the red leads towards roots, dyeing knowledge and the people who keep it alive.
descriptions./textiles/tasar/: Before the border and the drape, there is a cocoon. Follow Tasar from branch to yarn, then towards the places and people who give the silk its next life.

Content Navigability and Structure ### Landmarks - **Place all content within landmarks:** Wrap each relevant part of the page in `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`, and `<footer>` elements so assistive-tech users can jump between regions. (1.3.6 Identify Purpose (Level AAA)) - **Use the correct landmark:** Use the `<header>` element as a container for introductory content, the `<nav>` element as a container for site-wide or in-page navigation links, the `<main>` element as a container for the main content of the page, the `<aside>` element as a container for content that is tangentially related to the main content, and the `<footer>` element as a container for information about the related content, such as the author, copyright information, and links to related documents. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Use one `<main>` landmark per page:** Avoid using multiple `<main>` elements on a single page. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Provide distinguishable accessible names for navigation regions:** If a page contains multiple `<nav>` elements, apply the `aria-label` attribute to each element and set its value to a distinguishable accessible name for the region. For example: `<nav aria-label="Primary">`, `<nav aria-label="Secondary">`, and so on. (Best practice) - **Don't overuse landmarks:** Too many landmarks dilute their value. In particular, avoid labeling a `<section>` (which turns it into a `region` landmark) — `region` should be a last resort when no other landmark fits. (Best practice) ### Headings - **Structure main content with headings:** Use `<h1>`–`<h6>` elements sequentially so screen reader users get a navigable outline. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't use "fake" headings:** Never use `<div>` or `<span>` elements to look like headings without standard `<h1>`–`<h6>` elements. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Avoid nesting headings incorrectly:** Make sure that, if a sub-heading is visually less important than its parent heading, its heading level is lower in the heading hierarchy. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Use one `<h1>` element per page:** Use the `<h1>` element for the page's main heading. Having more than one `<h1>` element on a page makes it difficult for screen reader users to identify the actual main heading. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** If a page includes a modal dialog that is marked up using the `<dialog>` element, `role="dialog"`, or `role="alertdialog"`, it is fine to mark up its main heading using the `<h1>` element because the dialog is a new window that is separate from the page. - **Avoid "skipped" heading levels:** Avoid jumping directly from (for example) `<h1>` → `<h4>` to avoid breaking the logical hierarchy. (Best Practice) - **Avoid placing headings inside the `<summary>` element:** Some browsers still expose this element as a button, which removes all roles from its children including headings. If a heading must act as a disclosure trigger, use an accordion or a disclosure implemented with ARIA where the heading element wraps the button, rather than use the `<details>` and `<summary>` elements. (Best Practice) ### Lists - **Use lists for repeated, contiguous content:** `<ul>`/`<ol>` give assistive tech a count of listitems up front and let users skip the entire list. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Use the correct list element:** Use the `<ul>` element for unordered lists where the order of the items is **not** important (such as a list of related products), and use the `<ol>` element for ordered lists where the order of the content **is** important (such as a list of instructions). (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Don't use lists for non-list content:** Do not use list markup to mark up separate paragraphs of text, as screen readers will announce list information when they encounter lists, therefore leading to a screen reader hearing potentially confusing and redundant information about the related content. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Don't use lists for checkboxes and radio buttons:** When marked up correctly, screen readers will already announce the number of checkboxes or radio buttons, as well as the number of the currently focused checkbox / radio button in the set, even though there is no list markup. Additional list markup will lead to duplication. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) ### Tables - **Do use the correct table elements:** Use the `<table>` element to identify the table, the `<caption>` element to provide a title and accessible name for the description, the `<tr>` element to identify individual rows in the table, and the `<th>` and `<td>` elements to identify header and data cells respectively. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Do use the `scope` attribute on `<th>` elements:** The `scope` attribute indicates whether the `<th>` element represents a row header (`<th scope="row">`) or a column header (`<th scope="col">`). (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't use tables for layout:** Screen readers will announce redundant information about the layout, which may be confusing for screen reader users, while the use of tabular markup has an impact on the reading and keyboard focus order of content. Use CSS Grid/Flexbox for visual layouts instead. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Avoid overly-complex tables:** Spanned rows, spanned columns, nested tables, and expandable / collapsible rows can make sense visually and meet the related WCAG success criterion, but the overall structure can be disorienting and difficult to navigate for screen reader users. In such cases, break tables up into smaller tables that are easier and more efficient to navigate. (Best Practice) ### Skip links - **Provide skip links** prior to repeated content like site headers with navigation or long/infinite lists, so that keyboard users can easily bypass them. (2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A)) - **Caveat:** Sometimes screen magnifiers do not follow the focus when a skip link’s target is not normally focusable. The recommended workaround is to make the target programmatically focusable, but not a part of the tab order, using `tabindex="-1"`. If the target contains focusable elements, this creates another usability issue as clicking within the target will always set the **sequential focus navigation start point** to the target rather than at a point between focusable elements. A solution that satisfies both user expectations is to make the first meaningful element within the intended target the actual target of the skip link with `tabindex="-1"`, for example a heading (`<h1 id="content" tabindex="-1">`). Beware that any content prior to such an element will be skipped, including other relevant content within the targeted section, and this creates usability gaps for other assistive tech users. - **Avoid using skip links where they are not needed:** A set of pages whose only common element is a single link to the Home page does not need a skip link. (Best Practice) - **Avoid overusing skip links:** A single skip link, or two skip links to cover the primary and secondary sets of common navigation links, is usually sufficient on a single page. Multiple unnecessary skip links add to the number of <kbd>Tab</kbd> stops to a page, which causes frustration for people who use the keyboard alone for navigation. (Best Practice) ```html <!-- Good: Skip to main content --> <a href="#content" class="skip-link">Skip to main content</a> <main id="content">...</main> ``` ### Code Example: good use of landmarks, headings, lists, tables, and a skip link ```html <!-- Good: Semantic landmarks, heading hierarchy, skip link --> <header> <a href="#platform-dashboard" class="skip-link visually-hidden">Skip to content</a> <nav aria-label="Primary"> <ul> <li><a href="/">Home</a></li> </ul> </nav> </header> <main> <h1 id="platform-dashboard" tabindex="-1">Platform Dashboard</h1> <section> <h2>User Statistics</h2> <table> <caption>Monthly active users</caption> <thead> <tr> <th scope="col">Month</th> <th scope="col">Users</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>January</td> <td>12,000</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3>Notes</h3> <ul> <li>Results do not include users without active subscriptions</li> <li>Results are accurate as of 31 December 2025</li> </ul> </section> </main> ``` ## 2. Semantic HTML and ARIA ### Prefer native HTML - **Prefer HTML elements and attributes to ARIA:** Avoid `<div role="button">` or `<a role="button">` and use `<button>` instead. Native HTML elements and attributes already have the correct role and behavior, including keyboard support, built-in by default. `<button>` already implies `role="button"`, `required` already implies `aria-required`, and no additional JavaScript is required to ensure the correct role and behavior is supported. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** ARIA is required when the related feature is not available in HTML, for example there are no HTML elements explicitly intended for building a tabbed navigation widget, but ARIA includes appropriate role and state properties for this purpose. - **Don't add redundant ARIA roles or properties:** Avoid `<ul role="list">`, `<nav role="navigation">`, and `<input required aria-required="true">`. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** Safari removes list semantics from `<ul>`/`<ol>` outside `<nav>` when `list-style: none` or `display: flex`/`grid` is applied. In that case `role="list"` is required to restore them. - **Don't apply interactive ARIA roles to structural HTML elements:** Use `<li><span role="button">Button in a list</span></li>`, not `<li role="button">Button in a list</li>`, to avoid breaking the container list semantics. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Caveat:** It is acceptable to apply ARIA roles to structural HTML elements that have similar semantics, for example a tree view: `<ul role="tree"><li role="treeitem">…</li>…</ul>`. ### ARIA roles and states - **Match ARIA implementations to actual behavior:** When applying `role="tab"` to an element, it must then behave like a tab — including keyboard interactions. Many ARIA patterns can't be implemented in CSS alone and need JavaScript. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Manage toggle states:** Utilize `aria-expanded` and `aria-pressed` to communicate toggle states for custom controls. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Be deliberate about `disabled` vs `aria-disabled`:** `disabled` removes the element from the focus order entirely (and `tabindex="0"` won't bring it back), which is often wrong for toolbar buttons or links. `aria-disabled="true"` keeps the element focusable so users can land on it and learn it's disabled, but because it only communicates state to assistive technologies, you must also prevent activation (such as pointer clicks and keyboard triggers) in JavaScript. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't hide interactive elements from screen readers:** Do not apply `aria-hidden="true"` to interactive elements that receive focus, or to their parent elements. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Mandatory - Don't suppress the roles of interactive elements:** Applying `role="presentation"` or `role="none"` to an interactive element strips its semantics. The element will still be exposed to assistive technologies and announced by screen readers, but its role and any state information will not be, which results in confusion and potentially unexpected behavior. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Don't assume custom elements have no ARIA:** Custom elements can attach ARIA via `ElementInternals`, which some automated test tools can't see — so the absence of `role`/`aria-*` attributes in markup doesn't prove the element has no semantics. Verify with the browser's accessibility-tree inspector. (Best Practice) ## 3. Accessible Names and Descriptions Every interactive element and some landmarks need an accessible name, and many benefit from an accessible description. Names are short and identify the element; descriptions add context. ### Naming mechanisms - **Prefer native naming mechanisms:** `<label>` for form controls, `<caption>` for `<table>`, `<legend>` for `<fieldset>`, `<figcaption>` for `<figure>`. (Best Practice) - **Explicitly associate `<label>` with its control via `for`/`id`:** As well as ensuring the control is appropriately labeled by the contents of the `<label>` element, this results in a larger target area for people to activate the label _or_ its related control to move focus to the control, which isn't globally supported with other forms of labeling (such as using the `aria-labelledby` attribute). Additionally, some assistive technologies, particularly voice recognition software, require the `for`/`id` relationship to be explicitly set, even if an equivalent accessibility-supported approach (such as nesting an `<input>` inside a `<label>`) is taken. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Prefer `aria-labelledby` over `aria-label` when a visible label exists:** This avoids duplication, improves maintainability, and translates better. (Best Practice) - **Don't use `title` as a naming mechanism:** The value of this attribute is only displayed on mouse hover, and cannot be displayed or otherwise accessed using the keyboard in any browser. The contrast between `placeholder` text and its background in most browsers is very low, and therefore is difficult for people to perceive. (3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A)) - **Don't put `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` on elements that shouldn't be named:** Examples include plain `<div>`, `<span>`, and other custom elements without a role. These attributes are only intended for providing accessible names for elements that have explicit or implicit widget (for example, button, link, and tab), landmark, image, or iframe roles. (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - **Caveat:** Custom elements may have an implicit role set via `ElementInternals`, so the absence of a `role` attribute isn't conclusive. ### Choosing the name - **Avoid inconsistent link text:** If multiple hyperlinks direct users to the same target page, make sure each link has the same accessible name, which should typically be the same as its visible link text. For example, if the target page for a link is `profile.html`, make sure that all links have an accessible name of "My Profile" **or** "Profile"; do not use "My Profile" in one instance, and "Profile" in the other. While it may be visually obvious from the surrounding content what the purpose of these buttons might be, screen reader users may only hear "Edit, button". Techniques to resolve this include the following: (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Use visually hidden text:** The text is included in the DOM but is visually hidden using CSS. For example `<button>Edit <span class="visually-hidden">first name</span></button>`. The accessible name can include additional information before or after the visible text, but the visible text itself must not differ. For example, the accessible name for a link containing the link phrase "Read more" can be "Read more about [subject]", because the visible text is included without modification. However, the accessible name cannot be "Read some more about [subject]", because the term "some" appears between the words "Read" and "more", which is not reflected in the visible text. (2.5.3 Label in Name (Level A)) - **Don't reuse an accessible name across controls with different effects in the same view:** Make sure that each accessible name is disambiguated. (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)) - **Caveat:** Having two separate buttons with the accessible name of "Close" in two separate dialog boxes is fine, because only one dialog box is reachable at a time; however, multiple "Edit" buttons for different effects in the same dialog box is not. - **Don't reuse an accessible name across hyperlinks that point to different `href` targets:** For example, avoid `<a href="annualreport2025.html">Annual Report</a>` and `<a href="annualreport2026.html">Annual Report</a>`. Instead, use the `aria-describedby` attribute to programmatically associate any additional content with the field. For example: `<label for="yourComments">Your comments</label><p id="yourCommentsWarning">Please do not include any personal information in this field.</p><textarea id="yourComments" aria-describedby="yourCommentsWarning"></textarea>`. Screen readers will then announce the label first, followed by the control type, and only then announce additional information that a user can skip if they are already aware of it. (Best Practice) - **Don't repeat state information already exposed by ARIA inside the label:** Examples include information exposed via the `aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-selected`, `aria-pressed`, and similar attributes. This creates duplication, redundancy, and ambiguity. (Best Practice) - **Don't include the role name in the label:** This will lead to duplication. For example, `<nav aria-label="Primary navigation">` will be read by screen readers as "Primary navigation, navigation". (Best Practice) ### Descriptions - **Identify instructions, error messages, and any other important information explicitly related to a control as a description:** Examples of descriptions include: (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)) - A list of password requirements when creating an account - An error message related to a field in a previously submitted form - Additional instructions, such as "You must agree to the terms and conditions before you can submit the form" - **Make sure the description is available to assistive technologies when the related element receives focus:** Take one of the following approaches (1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)): - If the description is already visible on the page, programmatically associate it with the element using the `aria-describedby` attribute. - If the description is not visible on the page and is explicitly for screen reader users (in other words, when providing a visible description is not appropriate or useful), apply the `aria-description` attribute to the element and use it to provide an appropriate description. - **Avoid including a description for every element:** if the primary label already provides sufficient information (such as "First name"), any additional description is likely to be redundant. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** Inline error messages associated with controls, such as error messages below / above text fields, as well as secondary labels that should be announced when the element receives focus, are exceptions. - **Avoid including information in the description that is already provided by attributes applied to the element:** For example, including "This is a required field" as a description for an `<input>` element that already includes the `required` attribute will lead to duplicate announcements. (Best Practice) - **Caveat:** `aria-invalid="true"` is an exception; many screen readers announce "invalid" when they reach an `<input>` that includes this attribute set to `true`, which indicates that the field is in error. However, it does not indicate what the error is. In such cases, a description (the actual human readable error message) is required. This attribute should only be applied and set to true when the error message is present. - **Avoid including interactive elements in an `aria-describedby` target** unless the content of the element reads sensibly as a description on its own. Learn more.", where "Learn more" will be announced out of its intended context: `<p id="description">Please don't include personal information in this field. <a href="…">Learn more</a></p>`. Instead, only include the plain text in the referenced description: `<p><span id="description">Please don't include personal information in this field.</span> <a href="…">Learn more</a></p>`. ### Code Example: Visually Hidden Utility A `.visually-hidden` utility provides text for screen readers without rendering it visually.
